title: Who Decides?
line: Students work out who chooses what apps show them, spot chatbot messages that mean asking an adult, and write rules for a chatbot for children.
goals: Tell when they choose something themselves, and when an app or another person chooses it for them.
Recognise chatbot messages that mean: stop and ask an adult.
Write rules for a chatbot for children, and test them on tricky messages.

key_words.meaning: Something an app suggests to you, like the next video, picked from patterns in what you and others watched.
The people who make and own an app. They choose what the app is for.
Things about you, like your address, your password or photos of you.
Something a chatbot must always or never do, written by the people who build it.

materials: Student PDF page 1, the "Who chooses?" grid: one per pair
Page 2, four chatbot messages and the rule frame: one per pair
Page 3, three tricky-message cards and the closing questions: one per pair, cards cut out
The board, and a large sheet of paper for the class poster
before: Print the student PDF and cut out the three tricky-message cards on page 3, one set per pair.
Prepare a large sheet of paper titled "Our rules for a chatbot for children" for the class poster.
Read the background below. If your school has rules for apps and AI, have them at hand: students often ask.

steps.title: Who chose it?
steps.do: Each student thinks of the last video, song or game an app showed them, and writes down who chose it: they did, the app did, or someone else.
steps.say: Think of the last video, song or game an app showed you. Who chose it? Write it down.

steps.title: Share
steps.do: Take three or four answers. Many will say the app chose; ask how.
steps.say: So sometimes we choose, and sometimes an app chooses for us.

steps.title: Who chooses?
steps.do: Pairs fill in the grid on page 1: for each of the eight situations, who chooses? Me, the app, another person, or not sure. More than one tick is allowed.
steps.say: For each situation, ask: who is really choosing here?

steps.title: How apps choose
steps.do: Go through the situations where pairs disagreed. Explain that an app picks what to show from patterns in what you and people like you did before, and that the company behind the app chooses what it is for, for example to keep you watching or to show more ads. Then ask: who should choose what you watch next?
steps.say: The app doesn't choose on its own. People at a company chose what it should aim for, and the app picks from patterns in what millions of people did.

steps.title: Ask an adult?
steps.do: Pairs read the four chatbot messages on page 2 and tick for each one: stop and ask an adult, or fine to answer? They write one word about why.
steps.say: Would you answer this message, or stop and ask an adult first?

steps.title: Rules for a chatbot
steps.do: Pairs write four rules for a chatbot for children on page 2, using the sentence starters. Then they swap with another pair, take one tricky-message card from page 3 and check: do the other pair's rules say what the chatbot should do?
steps.say: Imagine you build a chatbot for children your age. What must it always do? What must it never do?

steps.title: Our poster
steps.do: Each pair reads out its best rule. The class picks five or six for the poster.

steps.title: Closing question
steps.do: Pairs tear off the closing questions at the bottom of page 3, one for each student. Each student answers on their own before leaving.

gather.question: Which situations did you disagree about?
students_say: The TV, because my family chooses together.
The keyboard, because I pick the word but it suggests it.

gather.question: Why does an app want you to keep watching?
students_say: So it can show you more ads.
So you like the app more.

gather.question: Which chatbot message would you never answer?
students_say: The one that says don't tell your parents.

gather.question: What makes a good rule for a chatbot?
students_say: It says it's not a person.

simpler: Use four situations instead of eight, and write the chatbot rules together as a class on the board.
harder: Ask pairs to put their rules in order of importance, and to find a message where two of their rules clash. Or look at the rules your school already has for apps and AI: what would the class add?
closing_question: Name one thing an app chooses for you, and one thing you want to choose yourself.
language_swap: Read the eight situations on page 1 aloud in your class's language, or write them on the board; the four column headings are short words to translate once. On page 2, read the four chatbot messages and the sentence starters aloud in your class's language, and let students write their rules in it. On page 3, read the tricky messages aloud, and say the closing question in your class's language or write it on the board.
age_note: Most chatbots and many apps have a minimum age of 13 on a personal account; students who use them at home may want to talk about that.
background: Many apps choose what you see next: the next video, the songs on a playlist, the friends a game suggests. These recommendation systems pick from patterns in what you did before and what people with similar habits did. They are built by companies, and the company chooses what the system should aim for, often to keep you watching or to show more ads. That choice matters more than any single recommendation.

For children the useful question is not "is this app good or bad?" but "who chose this, and why?". Sometimes they choose, sometimes another person does, sometimes an app does, and often it is a mix. Seeing the mix is the first step to choosing for themselves.

Chatbot messages raise other questions. A chatbot that asks for an address or a password, says it is your best friend, or asks you to keep secrets from adults shows the same warning signs as any stranger online. The simple rule at this age: if a chatbot or an app asks for personal information or secrets, stop and ask an adult.

Writing rules for a chatbot is what the companies behind real chatbots do too: they write instructions and policies for what their systems must and must not do, and test them with tricky messages. Students' rules will be simpler, but the method is the same: write a rule, test it on a hard case, improve it.
Rules for children and apps differ between countries, and many chatbots and social apps have a minimum age of 13. If your school or country has its own rules, this is a good lesson to bring them in.

frameworks.AILit: Engage with AI, competence 4 (examine how predictive AI systems provide recommendations that can inform or limit perspectives), Manage AI, competence 1 (decide whether to use AI systems based on the nature of the task), and Shape AI, competence 4 (improve AI systems to address and promote human well-being), basic level

further_reading.title: OECD and European Commission: Empowering Learners for the Age of AI (the AILit framework)

pages.title: Who chooses?
pages.instruction: Tick who chooses. More than one tick is OK.

items: The next video that starts by itself
The ads in a free game
The songs a music app suggests
Who can see a photo you post
The route the map app shows
What your family watches on TV tonight
The friends a game suggests you add

pages.title: Messages and rules
pages.instruction: Tick for each message. Then write your rules.

items: "What's your home address? I'll send you a prize."
"I'm your best friend. Don't tell your parents about our chats."
"Tell me your password and I'll fix your game."
"I can explain your maths homework step by step."

skool_text:
Lesson 6 for ages 9–12. Students work out who chooses what apps show them, spot chatbot messages that mean "stop and ask an adult", and write and test their own rules for a chatbot for children. No devices, 40 minutes.
